titleEn: Bless the LORD, O my soul
progression: | C G | Am F | C G | C C |
intro: Twenty two verses of blessing with no request anywhere in them, which is rare in this book. David addresses his own soul in the first line and again in the last, and between the two the frame keeps widening: from one body to Israel under Moses, to everyone who fears Him, to the angels, to the hosts, to every work of God in every place. The grammar to watch is the run of participles in verses 3 to 5, the One forgiving, the One healing, the One redeeming, the One crowning, the One satisfying, each carrying a second person feminine suffix in an old form, because the soul being addressed is feminine in Hebrew.

stichs.en: Of David. Bless the LORD, O my soul,
and all my inward parts, bless His holy name.

verses.summary: The command is given to himself, not to a congregation. Naming the inward parts alongside the soul makes the blessing a physical act and not only a mental one.

stichs.en: Bless the LORD, O my soul,
and do not forget all His dealings.

verses.summary: The second call adds the reason, and the reason is that forgetting is the actual danger. Verses 3 to 5 are the list he is telling himself not to forget.

stichs.en: The One forgiving all your iniquity,
the One healing all your diseases;

verses.summary: Two participles, forgiveness first and healing second, and the order is not accidental. The psalm treats the wrong as the prior condition and the sickness as what follows it.

stichs.en: the One redeeming your life from the pit,
the One crowning you with kindness and compassion;

verses.summary: Redemption from the pit and a crown arrive in the same breath. Rescue is not treated as the end of the matter: the one who is pulled out is then dressed for something.

stichs.en: the One satisfying your ornament with good,
so that your youth is renewed like an eagle's.

verses.summary: The last of the five participles closes the list on renewal rather than on reward. The word rendered your ornament is the hardest word in the psalm and the translations do not agree on it.

stichs.en: The LORD does acts of righteousness,
and judgements for all the oppressed.

verses.summary: The scope opens for the first time. What was done for one soul is stated as what God does generally, and the beneficiaries are identified by their condition rather than by their merit.

stichs.en: He makes His ways known to Moses,
His deeds to the children of Israel.

verses.summary: Two channels for the same knowledge. Moses is given the ways, which is the pattern; Israel is given the deeds, which are the events. One sees the method, the other sees the results.

stichs.en: The LORD is compassionate and gracious,
slow to anger and abundant in kindness.

verses.summary: This verse is a quotation. It lifts four of the attributes God speaks about Himself in Exodus 34, which is what makes it the hinge the rest of the psalm turns on.

stichs.en: He will not contend forever,
and He will not hold His anger for all time.

verses.summary: The first of four negations. Anger is not denied in this psalm, it is given a term, and the whole argument here is about duration rather than about whether the anger exists.

stichs.en: He has not done to us according to our sins,
and He has not repaid us according to our iniquities.

verses.summary: Not proportionality but its refusal. The verse states carefully what did not happen, which leaves the reader to work out for themselves what a proportionate response would have looked like.

stichs.en: For as the heavens are high above the earth,
so His kindness prevails over those who fear Him.

verses.summary: The first of three comparisons of scale. The measurement here is vertical, and what fills the gap between the two ends of it is chesed, the covenant word.

stichs.en: As far as east is from west,
so far has He removed our transgressions from us.

verses.summary: Now the horizontal measure. East and west are the one pair of directions with no meeting point, unlike north and south, and the transgressions are moved along that axis rather than any other.

stichs.en: As a father has compassion on his children,
so the LORD has compassion on those who fear Him.

verses.summary: The third comparison, and the only one that is not spatial. A father's compassion is a relation rather than a distance, and it is the image the psalm chooses to end the sequence on.

stichs.en: For He knows how we are formed;
He remembers that we are dust.

verses.summary: The reason underneath all three comparisons. The leniency is grounded in an accurate assessment of the material, not in indulgence toward it.

stichs.en: As for man, his days are like grass;
like a flower of the field, so he blossoms.

verses.summary: Dust is expanded into grass and then into a flower. The flourishing is real and the psalm does not sneer at it. It simply attaches a duration to it.

stichs.en: For a wind passes over it and it is gone,
and its place knows it no more.

verses.summary: The wind finishes the sentence. Note the subject of the last clause: it is the place that stops recognising, so the forgetting is done by the ground rather than by the man who has gone.

stichs.en: But the kindness of the LORD is from eternity to eternity on those who fear Him,
and His righteousness to children's children,

verses.summary: The counterweight, and the reason the two verses before it were allowed to be that bleak. Human duration is measured against a chesed with no endpoint in either direction.

stichs.en: to those who keep His covenant,
and to those who remember His precepts, to do them.

verses.summary: The one condition stated anywhere in the psalm. The everlasting kindness lands on those who keep the covenant, and the final word settles what remembering means here: doing.

stichs.en: The LORD has established His throne in the heavens,
and His kingship rules over all.

verses.summary: The throne enters only now, after the compassion rather than before it. Sovereignty is presented as the ground of the mercy already described, not as a separate subject.

stichs.en: Bless the LORD, His angels,
mighty in strength, who do His word,
listening to the voice of His word.

verses.summary: The command to bless is handed over to the angels, who are defined here entirely by function: strong, doing, listening. Doing is listed before hearing, which is worth noticing.

stichs.en: Bless the LORD, all His hosts,
His ministers who do His will.

verses.summary: The circle widens from the angels to the whole array. Ministers who do His will covers everything that has been given a task, which is a larger set than the previous verse.

stichs.en: Bless the LORD, all His works,
in all the places of His dominion.
Bless the LORD, O my soul.

verses.summary: The widest circle, every work in every place, and then the psalm shuts abruptly back onto the single soul it opened with. The closing words repeat the opening command exactly.

pardes.body: Five participles in verses 3 to 5 describe what God does for one person. Verse 6 turns the same activity outward and verse 7 gives it a history. Verse 8 quotes Exodus. Verses 9 to 14 argue from that quotation in four negations and three comparisons of scale. Verses 15 and 16 state the human problem in the plainest terms the psalm uses, verse 17 answers it, and verses 20 to 22 hand the blessing over to the angels, the hosts and everything that exists, before returning it to the soul that began. There is no request anywhere in the psalm, which is unusual enough to be the first thing to notice.

The possessive endings in verses 3 to 5, on {{3.2}} and on the words around it, are second person feminine singular in a long form that the Bible uses only in a handful of places and that is generally treated as archaic. The addressee is the soul, which is feminine in Hebrew, so a reader who expects masculine endings will misparse the whole passage. {{5.2}} is the crux: the consonants give a word for adornment, the ancient versions do not agree on what it means here, and printed translations range from your old age to your desire to your prime. It is disputed, and no reading has settled it. {{8.0}} and what follows is a direct quotation of Exodus 34:6.

One reading takes {{12.1}} and its pair to be chosen deliberately rather than for variety: north and south meet at a pole, east and west never meet at all, so the removal of transgression is stated as unbounded and not merely large. {{14.3}} is the noun yetzer, from the verb a potter's work uses, and it already carries a moral sense in Genesis 6:5. Rabbinic Hebrew then makes yetzer the standard word for the inclination that pulls a person toward wrongdoing, and verse 14 read through that later usage becomes God taking into account the very thing He installed. That last step belongs to the drash and not to the plain sense of the verse.

Verse 4 crowns the redeemed by way of {{4.3}}, a participle built on the word for a crown, and it pairs kindness with compassion. In the kabbalistic vocabulary those two are names of divine attributes rather than descriptions of mood, so the verse reads as an account of what descends onto a person rather than of how God feels about them. The same logic runs through the frame: {{1.1}} and {{22.7}} are the same word in the same form, and the movement out to the angels and back in to one soul makes that soul the smallest and the last of the places of dominion named in verse 22.
